subject: maths
title: Area of composite shapes and trapeziums

scenes.heading: Area of composite shapes and trapeziums
scenes.say: Skateboard ramps, garden beds and L-shaped rooms are not plain rectangles. So how do you find their area? Let's learn the trapezium formula and some smart tricks for composite shapes.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Level a sloping sand wall: 6 cm and 10 cm high becomes 8 cm all along
scenes.science: A trapezium has the same area as a rectangle of its average width
scenes.breaks: Sand can move anywhere, but a trapezium's height must be measured at right angles to its parallel sides.
scenes.say: Imagine a sand wall that is six centimetres high at one end and ten at the other. Smooth the top flat and it ends up eight centimetres high all along, the average. A trapezium works the same way: its area equals a rectangle as wide as the average of its parallel sides.

scenes.heading: Parts of a trapezium
notes: a and b are the parallel sides
scenes.say: First the trapezium is drawn. The arrows show its two parallel sides, a on top and b on the bottom. Then the dashed height, h, drops straight down at a right angle. The sloping sides are never the height.

scenes.heading: Why the formula works
scenes.say: Take two copies of the trapezium and turn one upside down. Together they make a parallelogram with base a plus b and height h. The trapezium is exactly half of it.

scenes.heading: The trapezium formula
parts: because it is half a parallelogram
scenes.say: So the area is a half, times a plus b, times h. Add the parallel sides, multiply by the height, then halve.
scenes.caption: A = ½ × (a + b) × h. Add the parallel sides, multiply by the height, then halve.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 5 cm.
scenes.say: Parallel sides six and ten, height five. Six plus ten is sixteen. Sixteen times five is eighty. Half of eighty is forty. The area is forty square centimetres.
scenes.caption: Parallel sides 6 and 10, height 5. 6 + 10 = 16. 16 × 5 = 80. Half of 80 is 40. Area = 40 cm².

scenes.heading: Composite shapes: add or subtract
scenes.say: Here is an L-shaped floor. Draw the big fourteen by ten rectangle around it, that's one hundred and forty, then subtract the missing six by four corner: one hundred and sixteen square metres. Or split it with the dashed line and add the two pieces. Same answer, so it checks out.
scenes.caption: Big rectangle 14 × 10 = 140, minus the missing 6 × 4 = 24, gives 116 m². Or split with the dashed line and add: 84 + 32 = 116 m².

scenes.heading: Two more tricks
points: Kite or rhombus: A = ½ × d₁ × d₂
Paths and frames: add the width TWICE
scenes.say: Two more tricks. A kite or rhombus is half the rectangle made by its diagonals, so multiply the diagonals and halve. For a path or frame, the width goes on both sides. And if you know the area, put the numbers in the formula and solve for the missing length.

points: Height meets the parallel sides at 90°
Kite or rhombus: ½ × d₁ × d₂
Check one method with the other
scenes.say: Quick recap. Trapezium area is a half times a plus b times h, using the perpendicular height. Kites and rhombuses use half the product of the diagonals. For composite shapes, add pieces or subtract a missing piece, and check one way with the other. Now try the practice questions!
